newsitem.title: SWEDEN: Astra says stockpiling won't hit full yr.
newsitem.headline: Astra says stockpiling won't hit full yr.

text.p: Swedish drugs company Astra's chief executive Hakan Mogren said stockpiling and currency fluctuations would not have a significant effect on full-year earnings.

Mogren's statement came after Astra posted a first quarter result that disappointed the market, saying stockpiling by patients and wholesalers prior to year-end 1996 had taken its toll on sales and earnings.

A pre-tax profit of 3.46 billion crowns, posted on Monday, was below an expected 3.93 billion crowns and the report sent Astra's shares plunging on the Stockholm Stock Exchange, down 22 crowns to 320.5 crowns.
"I would say that the effect (of stockpiling) on earnings is roughly some hundreds of million of crowns," Mogren said.
The negative impact on sales amounted to about 400 million crowns, Astra said earlier.
Sales rose nine percent in the three months ending March 31 to 10.13 billion crowns with sales of its top selling drug, anti-ulcer treatment Losec rising 14 percent to 4.80 billion crowns.
Mogren said the stockpiling effect should have ended after the first quarter.
He said difficulties in figuring out how much foreign exchange would impact earnings could also help explain why analysts expected a higher profit.
"The market does not know exactly how our currency hedging looks," he said.
Because of hedging, the softer Swedish crown did not have an immediate impact on earnings, Astra said in its report.
Mogren told Astra's annual general meeting late on Monday that the company was conducting two follow-ups to its blockbuster anti-ulcer agent Losec which were currently being tried out on humans.

"We are developing follow-ups to Losec which will have medical advantages...give us a product range with different products for different categories of patients and...give us renewed patent protection for these products," Mogren said.
"Two such follow-ups are currently being tested on humans."
Mogren expected these agents to reduce the negative effect on sales when Losec patents start expiring in 2001.
"The idea is to be able to launch follow-ups so we reduce a dip when the patent expires," Mogren said.
Mogren refrained, for competition reasons, from disclosing details about the drugs.
